title: Growth and Development: Definitions and Principles
body:
## What it is
- **Growth** is the physical, measurable increase in size of the body or its parts. Weight is the best single index of growth. It happens mostly in the first 20 years, fastest in infancy, with a second spurt in adolescence.
- **Development** is the qualitative gain in function, complexity and skill. It can continue after growth stops.
- **Maturation** is the built-in, genetically programmed unfolding of development.
- Growth and development are separate but linked processes.

## Must-know principles
- Continuous from conception to death; always in a set order.
- **Uneven pace**: fast in infancy and adolescence, slower in between.
- **Asynchronous**: body systems grow at different rates. Neurologic tissue peaks in the first year, genital tissue stays small until puberty.
- **Cephalocaudal**: head to tail. A newborn lifts only the head when prone; by about 2 months the chest lifts too.
- **Proximal to distal**: from the midline outward, so shoulder control comes before finger control.
- **Gross to refined**: large-muscle skills come before fine ones (a 3-year-old colors with a fat crayon; a 12-year-old writes with a fine pen).
- There is an optimal time for learning: a child cannot learn a task until the nervous system is mature enough.

## How the exam asks about it
Questions give a behavior and ask whether it is expected for age, or which principle explains it. Rule of thumb: ask which direction the skill travels (head first, center first, big first).

## Related topics
[[Childhood Age Periods and Developmental Theories]], [[Infant Development, Fears and Play]], [[Maternal and Child Health]]

title: Childhood Age Periods and Developmental Theories
body:
## Age periods (as given in the handout)
- Neonate: first 28 days. Infant: 1 month to 1 year. Toddler: 1 to 3 years. Preschooler: 4 to 6 years (other parts of the handout say 3 to 5). School-age: 7 to 12 years. Adolescent: 13 to 18 years.

## Freud (psychosexual) vs Erikson (psychosocial)
- Infant: Oral stage; trust vs mistrust (to love and be loved).
- Toddler: Anal stage; autonomy vs shame and doubt (be independent, decide for self).
- Preschool: Phallic stage; initiative vs guilt (start things, problem solving).
- School-age: Latent stage; industry vs inferiority (do things well).
- Adolescent: Genital stage; identity vs role confusion (who am I, adjusting to body image).

## Piaget and Kohlberg in one line each
- Piaget: sensorimotor (infant), preoperational (about 2 to 7), concrete operational (7 to 12), formal operational (12 and up).
- Kohlberg: pre-conventional (toddler/preschool, punishment and reward), conventional (school-age, wanting to be seen as good), post-conventional (adolescent and older, social contract and principles).

## Other facts
- **Maternal bonding** is best started right after birth and can be achieved within the first 30 minutes.
- Vocabulary listed: about 900 words at 3 years, 1500 at 4, 2100 at 5.

## Memory aid
Erikson's words in order: Trust, Autonomy, Initiative, Industry, Identity (made-up aid: "T-A-I-I-I").

## Related topics
[[Growth and Development: Definitions and Principles]], [[Infant Development, Fears and Play]], [[Toddler Development and Toilet Training]], [[Freud's Theory and Defense Mechanisms]]

## Check against your textbook
- Preschool age is given as 3-5 and 4-6 in different places; most texts use 3 to 5 or 6. Check the vocabulary numbers.

title: Infant Development, Fears and Play
body:
## What it is
- Age birth to 1 year (the handout table says 1 month to 1 year; the first 28 days are the neonate). Growth and development are very rapid.

## Must-know facts
- **Fear**: stranger anxiety. **Play**: solitary. **Toys**: mobiles, rattles, musical toys, crib toys (sensory toys).
- **Freud**: oral phase; pleasure from sucking and mouth stimulation.
- **Erikson**: trust versus mistrust; the task is to love and be loved.
- **Piaget (sensorimotor)**: 1-4 months primary circular reactions (body is the center); 4-8 months secondary circular reactions (from body to environment); 8-12 months coordination of secondary reactions; 12-18 months tertiary circular reactions (trial and error).
- **Moral development (handout)**: a pre-moral or pre-religious stage; infants learn that some actions bring approval and others scolding.

## Assessment
- Compare head control, sitting, grasping and social responses with age; watch bonding and feeding.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Meet oral needs: safe, washable toys and a pacifier.
2. **Feed on demand**, following the infant's biologic need for food.
3. When oral feeding is not allowed but sucking is, give a pacifier. Why: non-nutritive sucking is a real comfort need.
4. Give consistent caregiving so trust forms; respond to cries.
5. Keep toys too large to swallow and keep small objects away (safety).

## Complications and red flags
- Poor feeding, little eye contact, failure to gain weight, delayed head control.

## Client teaching
- Teach parents about feeding on demand, safe toys, holding and talking to the baby.

## How the exam asks about it
- Pick the toy for an infant: sensory (mobile, rattle). Pick the response to stranger anxiety: keep the parent or a familiar caregiver near.

## Memory aid
Infant = Trust (T for Tiny, Touch).

## Related topics
[[Childhood Age Periods and Developmental Theories]], [[Toddler Development and Toilet Training]], [[Newborn Reflexes]], [[Piaget's Stages of Cognitive Development]]

## Check against your textbook
- Confirm exact ages for sensorimotor sub-stages.

title: Toddler Development and Toilet Training
body:
## What to know
- Age 1 to 3 years; growth alternates between fast and slow bursts.
- **Fear**: separation anxiety. **Play**: parallel (side by side, not together). **Toys**: push-and-pull toys.
- Typical look: pot belly and bow legs. Asks questions constantly. All 20 deciduous teeth are present by about 3 years.
- Freud: anal phase. Erikson: autonomy vs shame. Piaget: preoperational thought begins (symbolic, concrete, literal, egocentric). Kohlberg: pre-conventional, behavior driven by punishment and reward.

## Readiness for toilet training (all must fit the child, not the calendar)
- Stays dry about 2 hours or wakes dry from a nap.
- Can sit, squat and walk; can remove clothing.
- Recognizes the urge to urinate or defecate.
- Wants to please the parent.
- Sits on the toilet 5 to 10 minutes without fussing.

## Negativism
Toddlers say "no" to test independence. Nursing response:
- Offer choices (limited ones).
- Avoid yes/no questions; use open-ended wording.

## Sleep
A consistent bedtime ritual and a security object help.

## Related topics
[[Infant Development, Fears and Play]], [[Preschooler Development and Thinking]], [[Therapeutic Communication]]

title: Preschooler Development and Thinking
body:
## What it is
- Age about 3 to 5 years (handout; the age table says 4 to 6). The child grows about 2.5 to 3 inches per year.

## Must-know facts
- **Fear**: mutilation and castration (fear of body injury). **Play**: associative and imitation or make-believe. **Toys**: simple puzzles, dolls, coloring books.
- **Freud**: phallic stage; awareness of the genital area. **Oedipus complex**: a preschool boy's strong attachment to his mother. **Electra complex**: a girl's attachment to her father.
- **Erikson**: initiative versus guilt; the task is to start doing things (basic problem solving) and learn that doing things is desirable.
- **Piaget**: preoperational thought; symbolic, concrete, literal.
  - **Centering**: sees only one feature of an object (the banana is yellow but not long).
  - **Magical thinking**: animals and objects can think and feel.
  - **Egocentrism**: own thoughts and needs seem more important than others'.
- **Kohlberg**: pre-conventional, stage 2; acts to satisfy own needs.
- By 5 years, mealtimes become social: conversation, manners, and willingness to try new foods.
- Vocabulary: about 900 words at 3 years, 1500 at 4, 2100 at 5 (handout).

## Assessment
- Compare language, play with others, toilet independence, fears, and self-care skills with age.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Use short, simple, concrete words; show the equipment and let the child handle it.
2. Reassure that treatment is not a punishment. Why: magical thinking leads to guilt.
3. Allow make-believe play with dolls to rehearse procedures.
4. Use bandages and explain which body part is involved; protect privacy.
5. Offer simple choices.

## Complications and red flags
- Extreme fears, regression, or sleep problems after hospitalization.

## Client teaching
- Teach parents about patience with questions, gentle limits, imaginative play and encouragement of initiative.

## How the exam asks about it
- A preschooler thinks illness is punishment: answer reassures and explains simply.

## Related topics
[[Toddler Development and Toilet Training]], [[School-Age Child Development]], [[Piaget's Stages of Cognitive Development]], [[Fears, Play and Toys by Age Group]]

## Check against your textbook
- Preschool age is given as 3-5 and 4-6 in different places. Confirm.

title: School-Age Child Development
body:
## What it is
- Age about 6 to 12 years (the handout's age-period table says 7 to 12). Growth and development are slow and steady.

## Must-know facts
- **Fear**: displacement from school (being kept out). **Play**: indoor competitive. **Toys**: computer games and table games.
- **Freud**: latent phase, when personality development appears dormant and the child's energy goes into concrete thinking.
- **Erikson**: industry versus inferiority; the task is to do things well.
- **Piaget**: concrete operations (7 to 12). Systematic reasoning, classifying by attributes such as color, and **reversibility** (retracing steps, like a maze backwards).
- **Reasoning is inductive**, specific to general: a plastic toy broke, so all plastic toys break easily.
- **Kohlberg**: conventional level (7 to 10); follows rules to be a "good" person in own and others' eyes.

## Assessment
- Compare school performance, friendships, self-esteem and independence with age expectations.
- Look for signs of feeling inferior or failing: refusing school, withdrawal, avoiding tasks.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Encourage achievement: give tasks the child can complete.
2. When hospitalized, keep up schoolwork and contact with classmates (fear of displacement).
3. Explain procedures step by step and logically; allow questions.
4. Use rules and fairness; the child accepts rules to be seen as good.
5. Offer table and computer games as suitable activity.

## Complications and red flags
- Persistent school refusal, bullying, withdrawal, or sudden decline in performance.

## Client teaching
- Teach parents to praise effort, set clear rules, and support hobbies and friendships.

## How the exam asks about it
- Choose the best activity or explanation for a school-age child: competitive indoor games, logical explanation, chances to finish tasks.
- Trap: using magical or oversimplified explanations meant for preschoolers.

## Memory aid
School-age = Industry (I work, I finish).

## Related topics
[[Preschooler Development and Thinking]], [[Adolescent Development]], [[Piaget's Stages of Cognitive Development]], [[Kohlberg's Stages of Moral Development]], [[Fears, Play and Toys by Age Group]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout gives 6-12 and 7-12 for this age group. Confirm.

title: Adolescent Development
body:
## What it is
- Age about 13 to 18 years: accelerated growth and maturation, driven by hormones.

## Must-know facts
- Growth spurt starts about 1 to 2 years earlier in girls than in boys.
- Sebaceous and sweat glands become active and fully functional (acne, body odor).
- **Fear**: displacement from peers. **Play**: outdoor competitive (athletics and sports). **Toys**: basketball and similar.
- **Freud**: genital phase; new sexual aims and new love objects.
- **Erikson**: identity versus role confusion; learning who they are by adjusting to body image.
- **Piaget**: formal operations (about 12 and up); hypothetical and scientific reasoning, understanding cause and effect, dealing with past, present and future.
- **Kohlberg**: post-conventional (older than 12); social contract and universal ethical principles. Many adults do not reach this level.
- Adolescents can take responsibility for self-care because they see it as adult behavior.

## Assessment
- Assess body image concerns, peer relationships, school, family conflict, risk behavior, mood.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Provide privacy and confidentiality (within safety limits).
2. Use "talk time" to sort through attitudes and feelings.
3. Involve the adolescent in decisions and self-care. Why: it supports identity and independence.
4. Keep contact with peers during hospitalization.
5. Explain in full, adult terms; respect questions.

## Complications and red flags
- Withdrawal, depression, eating problems, substance use, self-harm talk.

## Client teaching
- Teach healthy habits, acne and hygiene care, safe behavior, and how to reach help.

## How the exam asks about it
- The best intervention for a hospitalized adolescent supports peer contact and independence; not a toy or a long lecture to parents only.

## Related topics
[[School-Age Child Development]], [[Piaget's Stages of Cognitive Development]], [[Kohlberg's Stages of Moral Development]], [[Fears, Play and Toys by Age Group]], [[Therapeutic Communication]]

## Check against your textbook
- Confirm the ages for formal operations and puberty timing.

title: Apgar Score
body:
## What it is
- A quick assessment of the newborn's condition done at **1 and 5 minutes** after birth. Five criteria are each scored 0, 1 or 2, for a total of 10.

## Must-know facts
- **Appearance** (color): 0 blue, 1 acrocyanosis (pink body, blue hands and feet), 2 pink.
- **Pulse**: 0 absent, 1 under 100, 2 over 100.
- **Grimace** (reflex response): 0 no response, 1 grimace, 2 vigorous cry.
- **Activity** (muscle tone): 0 limp, 1 minimal flexion, 2 full flexion.
- **Respiration**: 0 absent, 1 weak cry, 2 vigorous cry.
- **Interpretation**: 8 to 10 good (healthy); 4 to 7 fair, needs observation, stimulation and suctioning; the handout says 1 to 3 poor, needs immediate resuscitation (most books give 0 to 3).

## Assessment
- Score at 1 minute and again at 5 minutes. Record each criterion. Keep rechecking if the score is low.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Dry, warm and position the airway; suction mouth then nose if needed (ABC: airway first).
2. Stimulate by rubbing the back or flicking the soles.
3. Support breathing and heart rate for low scores; begin resuscitation per policy if the score is 3 or less.
4. Keep warm and keep the baby with the mother if stable.
5. Document scores and actions.

## Complications and red flags
- Low heart rate, no breathing, poor tone, blue trunk: act immediately; do not wait for the 5-minute score.

## How the exam asks about it
- Compute the score from a description. Heart rate and breathing weigh most in deciding to act.
- A 1-minute score reflects how the baby tolerated birth; the 5-minute score reflects response to help.

## Memory aid
APGAR spells the five criteria: Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration.

## Related topics
[[Newborn Vital Signs and Heat Conservation]], [[EINC and Active Management of Third Stage of Labor]], [[Newborn Reflexes]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout starts poor at 1 rather than 0. Confirm the cutoffs for your exam.

title: Gestational Age Estimation and Newborn Measurements
body:
## Gestational age signs (premature vs full-term)
- **Skin**: premature is very thin, gelatinous with visible vessels; full-term is thick, leathery or cracked.
- **Lanugo** (fine hair): abundant in premature, thinning later, gone (bald) at full term.
- **Plantar creases**: only at the front in premature; whole sole at full term.
- **Breast**: barely any areola in premature; full areola at term.
- **Ear**: flat and folded in premature; thick and firm at term.
- **Genitals**: male, undescended testes in premature, fully descended at term. Female, prominent labia minora and clitoris in premature; covered by the labia majora at term.

## Measurements
- Normal birth weight 2.5 to 4.0 kg. Doubles at about 6 months, triples at 12 months, quadruples at about 2.5 years.
- **LBW** under 2500 g; **LGA** over 4000 g. Later-born children usually weigh more than the first-born.
- A newborn loses **5 to 10%** of birth weight in the first days because maternal salt and fluid-retaining hormones are gone.
- Length 46 to 54 cm. Head circumference 33 to 35 cm (the largest circumference in an infant). Chest 31 to 33 cm.

## Related topics
[[Newborn Vital Signs and Heat Conservation]], [[Newborn Assessment: Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, Neck and Chest]], [[Apgar Score]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's term "term" vs "full-term" columns is confusing (it reads as preterm, near-term, post-term). Confirm the stage each column means.

title: Newborn Reflexes
body:
## Reflexes and when they go
- **Extrusion**: food on the tongue is pushed out.
- **Tonic neck**: head turned to one side, arm and leg on that side extend, the opposite limbs flex. Fades by 3 to 4 months.
- **Palmar grasp**: finger in the palm is gripped. Lessens by 3 to 4 months.
- **Moro (startle)**: loud noise or sudden drop; arms symmetrically abduct and extend. Persisting beyond 6 months may suggest brain damage.
- **Sucking and rooting**: touching lip or cheek makes the baby turn, open the mouth and suck. Rooting usually fades by 3 to 4 months (may last up to 1 year).
- **Stepping (walking)**: held upright with a foot on a surface, baby steps. Present about 3 to 4 months.
- **Babinski**: stroke the sole from heel up the outer side; toes fan out and the big toe dorsiflexes. Disappears after about 1 year. **Absent Babinski** needs a neurologic exam.

## Why it matters
Reflexes show nervous system maturity. A reflex that is absent, asymmetric or persists too long is a red flag. Cerebral palsy often shows persistent primitive reflexes (see [[Cerebral Palsy]]).

## Related topics
[[Infant Development, Fears and Play]], [[Newborn Assessment: Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, Neck and Chest]]

title: Newborn Vital Signs and Heat Conservation
body:
## What it is
Normal newborn vital signs and how the newborn keeps warm.

## Must-know facts
- **Temperature**: axillary, 97.9 to 98 F (handout).
- **Apical heart rate**: 120 to 160 beats per minute.
- **Respirations**: 30 to 60 per minute, average 40.
- **Blood pressure**: about 73/55 mm Hg.
- Newborns **conserve heat** by constricting blood vessels, moving blood away from the skin.
- **Brown fat**, found in mature newborns, makes heat by raising metabolism. Premature infants have less brown fat.

## Assessment
- Take the apical rate for a full minute; count respirations for a full minute (they can be irregular); check axillary temperature; look for color, tone and breathing effort.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Dry the baby right away, cover the head, and keep skin-to-skin or under a radiant warmer. Why: wet skin loses heat fast.
2. Keep the nursery warm and away from drafts or cold surfaces.
3. Check temperature first when an infant looks unwell. Cold stress increases oxygen use and can lead to low blood sugar and breathing trouble.
4. Report fast breathing, grunting, retractions or nasal flaring (respiratory distress).

## Complications and red flags
- Hypothermia, hypoglycemia, apnea, respiratory distress.

## Client teaching
- Teach parents to dress the baby for the environment, avoid overbundling, and take temperatures correctly.

## How the exam asks about it
- A newborn with a low temperature: warm first, then evaluate for infection or low blood sugar.
- Trap: choosing to wait before warming.

## Related topics
[[Gestational Age Estimation and Newborn Measurements]], [[Apgar Score]], [[EINC and Active Management of Third Stage of Labor]]

## Check against your textbook
- Many texts give axillary temperature as about 36.5 to 37.5 C. Verify blood pressure and temperature ranges.

title: Newborn Assessment: Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, Neck and Chest
body:
## Head
- **Anterior fontanel**: soft, flat, diamond-shaped (3-4 cm by 2-3 cm); closes at 12 to 18 months.
- **Posterior fontanel**: triangular, about 0.5-1 cm; closes at 2 to 3 months.
- **Caput succedaneum**: scalp swelling from prolonged labor; **crosses suture lines**; gone in about 3 days.
- **Cephalhematoma**: blood under the periosteum from ruptured capillaries; does **not** cross suture lines (the usual rule; the handout does not say it); absorbs in 3 to 6 weeks.
- **Craniotabes**: localized soft or swollen cranial bone from pressure against the maternal pelvis; corrects itself.

## Eyes
- Permanent color settles between 3 and 12 months. Tear ducts mature by about 3 months. Strabismus is normal until 6 months. Subconjunctival hemorrhage (red spot on sclera) is absorbed in 2 to 3 weeks.

## Ears
- Top of the pinna should line up with the line from inner to outer canthus. **Low-set ears** suggest chromosomal disease (Down syndrome) or kidney anomaly.
- Hearing check: ring a bell about 6 inches from each ear.

## Nose
- Nasal flaring means respiratory distress. Test for choanal atresia by closing the mouth and blocking one nostril at a time; see [[Choanal Atresia]].

## Neck and chest
- Neck is short with skin folds. Rigidity may point to congenital torticollis or meningitis. The thymus is relatively large and triples in size by about 3 years.
- Chest is about 2 inches smaller than the head. **Retractions on inspiration are never normal**; they signal respiratory distress.

## Related topics
[[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]], [[Hydrocephalus]], [[Down Syndrome]]

## Check against your textbook
Cephalhematoma not crossing sutures is added textbook knowledge. The thymus size statement should be verified.

title: Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs
body:
## Abdomen and cord
- Slightly protruding abdomen is normal. A **scaphoid (sunken)** abdomen suggests missing contents (diaphragmatic hernia).
- Bowel sounds should be present within 1 hour of birth.
- Cord: white, gelatinous, **2 arteries and 1 vein**. A **single artery** may mean congenital heart, kidney or chromosomal anomaly. Falls off by day 6 to 10. Taping coins or buttons on an umbilical hernia does not help closure.

## Anus and genitalia
- Check the anus is present and patent. No stool in the first 24 hours: suspect imperforate anus or meconium ileus (see [[Duodenal Atresia and Imperforate Anus]]).
- Male: both testes in the scrotum; absent testes (cryptorchidism) call for a kidney work-up since both arise from similar tissue. Cremasteric reflex may be absent before 10 days. Urethral opening on the tip: dorsal opening is epispadias, ventral is hypospadias (see [[Hypospadias and Epispadias]]).
- Female: swollen vulva from maternal hormones; **pseudomenstruation** (mucus, sometimes blood-tinged) is normal.

## Back and limbs
- Pinpoint opening, dimple or sinus at the spine base suggests spina bifida occulta ([[Spina Bifida]]).
- Very short arms: achondroplasia. **Simian crease**: Down syndrome. Syndactyly (webbing) and polydactyly (extra digits) are noted.
- Hips: should flex and abduct nearly 180 degrees. Locking at 160 to 170 degrees suggests hip subluxation ([[Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip]]).

## Check against your textbook
The handout says the cremasteric reflex tests spinal nerves T8-T10; most texts say L1-L2. Verify.

title: Congenital Anomaly Appraisal in the Newborn
body:
## What it is
A screening checklist the nurse uses on a newborn to spot signs of a congenital anomaly. The findings are clues to report, not diagnoses.

## Must-know facts
- **Hydramnios** (too much amniotic fluid) suggests a **gastrointestinal obstruction**: the baby cannot swallow fluid. Examples: esophageal atresia, duodenal atresia.
- **Oligohydramnios** (too little) suggests a **genitourinary obstruction** or extreme prematurity.
- **Distended abdomen** suggests ascites, bowel obstruction, or a tumor.
- **Empty (scaphoid) abdomen** suggests a diaphragmatic hernia.
- **Passing a small catheter (no. 8) through the nares into the stomach**:
  - Fails through either nostril = **choanal atresia**.
  - Passes the nose but will not enter the stomach = **esophageal atresia**.
- **Counting umbilical vessels**: one artery suggests possible congenital urinary or cardiac anomalies or a chromosomal trisomy (if other findings agree).

## Assessment
- Review the maternal history (fluid level), inspect the abdomen, test patency, count the cord vessels, check the anus and genitalia.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Keep airway first: a baby with excessive drooling, choking or cyanosis with feeds needs immediate attention.
2. Do not feed until patency is checked when an atresia is suspected. Why: feeding can cause aspiration or vomiting.
3. Report abnormal findings to the provider and document.
4. Support the family with simple information.

## Complications and red flags
- Aspiration, respiratory distress, bile-stained vomit, absent stool.

## How the exam asks about it
- Match each clue to the condition: too much fluid -> GI blockage; too little -> kidney or urinary problem; one artery -> heart or kidney anomaly.

## Memory aid
Hydramnios -> Hole in the gut; Oligo -> Output (urine) problem (made-up aid).

## Related topics
[[Choanal Atresia]], [[Umbilical Cord Assessment]], [[Duodenal Atresia and Imperforate Anus]], [[Newborn Screening]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout does not explain esophageal atresia care; confirm.

title: Breastfeeding and Bottle-Feeding Safety
body:
## What it is
Safety teaching for parents about breast milk and formula feeding.

## Must-know facts
- **Almost all drugs pass into breast milk.** A breastfeeding mother must not take any medicine without checking with her primary care provider that it is compatible.
- **Do not warm bottles in a microwave**: the inner core of the milk can become very hot while the bottle feels cool.
- **Never prop a bottle**: it raises the risk of aspiration and otitis media, and takes away the pleasure of being held.
- **Do not put an infant to bed with a bottle**: this causes baby bottle syndrome (tooth decay). The handout says lower teeth; most books say upper front teeth.

## Assessment
- Ask how the baby is fed, positioned, and what medicines or supplements the mother takes.
- Observe a feeding for positioning, latch, and swallowing.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Hold the infant during every feed in a semi-upright position. Why: reduces aspiration and ear infection risk and supports bonding.
2. Teach safe warming: warm in a pan of warm water or under running warm water, mix and test on the wrist.
3. Teach the mother to check before taking any drug or herbal product.
4. Teach cleaning of the mouth and gums after feeds as the child grows.

## Complications and red flags
- Aspiration or choking, burns from overheated milk, ear infection, dental caries.

## Client teaching
- No propping, no bottle in bed, no microwave warming, review medicines with the provider.

## How the exam asks about it
- A mother says she leaves the bottle propped so she can cook: the best answer teaches the risks and offers holding the infant.

## Related topics
[[Infant Development, Fears and Play]], [[Maternal and Child Health]], [[Nutrition]]

## Check against your textbook
- Confirm the teeth affected in bottle caries and local advice on safe warming of milk.

title: Spina Bifida
body:
## What it is
Incomplete closure of the spinal column (neural tube defect), usually in the 4th week of embryonic life. Exact cause unknown; low maternal **folic acid** is a key factor, plus hereditary and environmental ones.

## Types
- **Occulta**: small dimple or tuft at the lower back; usually no symptoms or treatment.
- **Meningocele**: sac holding meninges and spinal fluid.
- **Myelomeningocele**: sac also holds spinal cord and nerves; the most severe. Associated problems: hydrocephalus, bowel and bladder dysfunction, lower-limb paralysis, meningitis.

## Priority nursing actions
- Protect the sac first: cover with a sterile, moist, non-adherent dressing; use aseptic technique (infection risk to the CNS).
- Position **prone** to reduce tension on the sac.
- Assess neurologic status, head circumference, fontanel fullness and ICP.
- Check the sac for redness, drainage, irritation; give antibiotics as ordered.
- Surgery is done as soon as possible, usually within 24 to 48 hours, to prevent meningeal infection.
- Anticholinergics for urinary continence, laxatives for bowel continence.

## Prevention and screening
- 600 micrograms folic acid daily for pregnant women (first trimester emphasis in handout).
- Raised AFP in maternal serum or amniotic fluid suggests an open spinal lesion. Women with a previous affected child are advised to have testing.

## Related topics
[[Hydrocephalus]], [[Bacterial Meningitis and Encephalitis]], [[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]]

## Check against your textbook
Folic acid timing: textbooks stress taking it before conception and early pregnancy. Latex precautions are often taught for these children but are not in the handout.

title: Hydrocephalus
body:
## What it is
Too much cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in the ventricles.
- **Communicating**: impaired absorption in the subarachnoid space.
- **Non-communicating (obstructive)**: flow blocked inside the ventricular system; blockage of the narrow aqueduct of Sylvius is the most common cause.
- Other causes: overproduction by the choroid plexus; risk factors include prior meningitis or encephalitis (adhesions), tumor or hemorrhage, Arnold-Chiari malformation, and meningocele surgery.

## Signs
- Bulging anterior fontanel, widely separated skull bones, "cracked-pot" sound on percussion (**Macewen's sign**), brow bulging (**bossing**), enlarging head circumference.

## Treatment: shunts
- **V-P shunt** (lateral ventricle to peritoneum) is the most used in children. A-V shunt goes to the right atrium. V-U shunt goes to the ureter and needs a nephrectomy.

## Nursing care
- Measure head circumference daily; protect the head; maintain nutrition and fluids.
- Pre-op: small frequent feedings until NPO, reposition the head often and use an egg-crate mattress, prepare family.
- Post-op: vital and neuro signs; lay the child on the **unoperated side** to avoid pressure on the valve; keep flat as prescribed to avoid sudden drainage; if ICP rises, raise the head of bed 15 to 30 degrees; watch for infection and drainage; intake and output.

## Related topics
[[Spina Bifida]], [[Bacterial Meningitis and Encephalitis]], [[Newborn Assessment: Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, Neck and Chest]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's HOB elevation advice for rising ICP and "keep flat" order conflict in spirit; follow the surgeon's orders and your textbook.

title: Bacterial Meningitis and Encephalitis
body:
## What it is
- **Meningitis**: inflammation of the membranes around brain and spinal cord. **Encephalitis**: inflammation of the brain itself.
- Bacterial causes: H. influenzae type B, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis; spread by droplets from the nose and throat. Viral causes: mumps, herpes, enteroviruses.

## Assessment
- Fever, irritability, change in consciousness, seizures.
- Stiff neck and **nuchal rigidity**; opisthotonus (arched back).
- **Kernig's sign**: cannot extend the leg when the thigh is flexed at the hip.
- **Brudzinski's sign**: neck flexion makes the hips and knees flex.
- Lumbar puncture: cloudy CSF, raised protein, **low glucose**; smear and culture find the organism.

## Priority nursing actions
1. **Isolate** the infant (first implementation on admission) to stop droplet spread.
2. Airway patent and safe during seizures.
3. Control temperature; neuro checks; watch level of consciousness.
4. Monitor for SIADH (fluid retention, cerebral edema, low sodium).
5. Intake and output, nutrition; identify close contacts for prophylaxis.

## Treatment
IV antibiotics. The handout names penicillin G; real choices depend on age and cultures.

## Related topics
[[Hydrocephalus]], [[Epiglottitis]], [[Sepsis and Septic Shock Recognition]]

## Check against your textbook
Penicillin G as "drug of choice" is oversimplified; broad-spectrum agents are typical until cultures return.

title: Cerebral Palsy
body:
## What it is
- A neuromuscular disorder with poor control of voluntary muscles, abnormal muscle tone, and incoordination. It is caused by damage to the developing brain, not a disease that worsens.

## Must-know facts
- **Anoxia to the brain** is the most significant factor in causation. Infection also contributes.
- Types by the brain area affected:
  - **Spastic** (most common): cortex; stiff muscles and a scissor-like gait, one foot crossing in front of the other.
  - **Athetoid**: basal ganglia; uncoordinated involuntary movements.
  - **Ataxic**: cerebellum; poor balance and difficulty with muscle coordination.

## Assessment
- Early signs: abnormal posturing, difficulty feeding, tremors or seizures, **persistence of primitive reflexes**, delayed motor development.
- Compare milestones: late head control, sitting, crawling, walking.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Promote adequate nutrition: feeding can be hard; position upright and allow time (risk of aspiration).
2. Keep a safe environment and seizure precautions.
3. Promote maximum mobility and self-help skills. Why: independence builds self-esteem and function.
4. Ensure safety during ambulation; use braces, crutches and walkers as prescribed.
5. Support the family with consistent teaching and referrals.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
- Exercises (passive and active), muscle relaxants, anticonvulsants, tranquilizers; braces and ambulation devices.

## Complications and red flags
- Seizures, aspiration, contractures, speech and hearing problems (added knowledge).

## Client teaching
- Teach parents the home exercise program, safe feeding, and medicine schedule; encourage school and play adapted to the child.

## How the exam asks about it
- Match type to brain area and sign. Persistent primitive reflexes past the expected age are a key early clue.

## Related topics
[[Newborn Reflexes]], [[Down Syndrome]], [[Developmental Disorders]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout does not mention a mixed type or intelligence level; confirm.

title: Down Syndrome
body:
## What it is
- **Trisomy 21**: a chromosomal aberration with an extra copy of chromosome 21, giving 47 chromosomes instead of 46.
- It is more common in children of mothers of advanced age.

## Must-know facts
- **Face**: wide gap between the eyes, flat nose, large tongue. **Head**: flattened front and back of the skull, flat occiput.
- **Hands and feet**: **simian crease** (single horizontal palm line); **plantar furrow** (vertical line on the sole); wide space between the first and second toes.
- **Brushfield's spots** (white specks in the iris), **low-set ears**, potbelly.
- Intelligence ranges from severely impaired to just below normal (the handout gives IQ under 20 to 50-70).
- Associated problems: congenital heart defects (VSD), Hirschsprung's disease, leukemia. Growth is reduced with rapid weight gain; sexual development may be delayed or incomplete.

## Assessment
- Newborn exam findings above; check for heart murmurs and feeding difficulties; watch growth and milestones.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Assess and stabilize any heart or breathing problem first.
2. Plan care by **developmental age**, not chronological age.
3. Provide consistent care so trust and security develop.
4. Aim for the child's best developmental potential and ability to cope.
5. Support the family emotionally; give honest, supportive information.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
- Treatment is supportive and aimed at associated problems (heart surgery if needed, nutrition, early stimulation, therapy).

## Complications and red flags
- Heart failure, breathing infections, bowel obstruction signs, leukemia signs (added knowledge).

## Client teaching
- Teach about early intervention, feeding and weight control, infection prevention, and community support.

## How the exam asks about it
- Identify the syndrome from the physical signs. The best nursing goal: help the child reach optimum development.

## Related topics
[[Ventricular and Atrial Septal Defects]], [[Hirschsprung's Disease]], [[Cerebral Palsy]], [[Congenital Torticollis, Achondroplasia and Digit Anomalies]]

## Check against your textbook
- Confirm IQ ranges and other conditions linked to Down syndrome; the handout wording is dated.

title: Congenital Heart Defects: Acyanotic Overview
body:
## What it is
Heart or vessel anomalies. **Acyanotic** defects either narrow a vessel or shunt blood **left to right** (oxygenated blood goes back to the lungs), so the child is not blue. Examples: VSD, ASD, PDA, pulmonary stenosis, coarctation of the aorta.

## General signs of heart disease in a child
- Tachycardia, tachypnea, profuse scalp sweating, fatigue, irritability.
- Feeding problems, poor weight gain or failure to thrive, frequent respiratory infections and cough.
- **Murmur** is the most common sign. Hepatomegaly from blood backing up. Sweating on the brow during feeding or crying.

## Complication
**Congestive heart failure** is the most common complication (moist cough, diaphoresis, severe dyspnea).

## Priority nursing thinking
Keep the child calm, small frequent feedings, conserve energy, watch for CHF, give digoxin and diuretics as ordered. Airway and oxygenation come first when the child is in distress.

## Related topics
[[Ventricular and Atrial Septal Defects]], [[Patent Ductus Arteriosus and Coarctation of the Aorta]], [[Pulmonary Stenosis]], [[Cyanotic Heart Defects and Tetralogy of Fallot]]
outlineRefs: Signs and Symptoms of heart disorders

title: Ventricular and Atrial Septal Defects
body:
## VSD
- Opening between the right and left ventricles; usually a left-to-right shunt. The most common congenital heart defect (about 30%).
- Overloads the right ventricle and lungs. Loud systolic murmur. Can lead to pulmonary hypertension, respiratory failure, and **Eisenmenger syndrome** (shunt reverses right to left).

## ASD
- Opening between the atria: failure of the atrial septum to close.
- Types: ostium primum (low), ostium secundum (center), sinus venosus (near the SVC).
- Small defects: no symptoms. Others: systolic ejection murmur, slow weight gain, right ventricular hypertrophy, tiring, respiratory infections. Heart failure is more likely with ostium primum.

## Treatment and nursing
- Small defects may close on their own.
- Non-surgical: closure device placed in cardiac catheterization. Surgical: open repair on bypass, ideally before school age.
- Teach the family about treatment options; monitor for CHF.

## Related topics
[[Congenital Heart Defects: Acyanotic Overview]], [[Down Syndrome]], [[Patent Ductus Arteriosus and Coarctation of the Aorta]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout says ASD defects are repaired mainly in girls because of pregnancy-related pulmonary hypertension. This is unusual; verify the indication. It also describes ASD as more oxygenated blood going right, which is the left-to-right shunt.

title: Patent Ductus Arteriosus and Coarctation of the Aorta
body:
## PDA
- The fetal ductus arteriosus fails to close after birth. Blood flows from the aorta back to the pulmonary artery, raising left ventricular work and lung congestion.
- Signs: loud **machinery-like murmur**, repeated respiratory infections, CHF (poor feeding, fatigue, tachypnea), poor weight gain, widening pulse pressure.
- Treatment: **ibuprofen or indomethacin** (prostaglandin synthetase inhibitors) can close it in premature infants. Otherwise close during catheterization or by surgery. Some close on their own.

## Coarctation of the aorta
- Narrowing of the aorta near the ductus.
- High blood pressure in the **arms** with headache, dizziness, nosebleeds; **weak or absent femoral pulses** (bounding radial pulse); leg cramps; systolic murmur.
- Treatment: digoxin and diuretics for CHF, balloon angioplasty, or surgical removal of the narrow part with end-to-end joining.

## Nursing focus
Compare arm and leg pulses and blood pressure; monitor for CHF.

## Related topics
[[Congenital Heart Defects: Acyanotic Overview]], [[Ventricular and Atrial Septal Defects]], [[Pulmonary Stenosis]]

title: Pulmonary Stenosis
body:
## What it is
- Narrowing at the entrance to the pulmonary artery (the pulmonary valve area). It is an acyanotic defect unless severe.
- Resistance to blood flow makes the right ventricle work harder, so it thickens (right ventricular hypertrophy), and less blood reaches the lungs. The right ventricle may even be underdeveloped.
- **Pulmonary atresia** is the extreme form: the valve leaflets are completely fused and no blood flows to the lungs.

## Must-know facts
- Pulmonary stenosis is one of the four parts of tetralogy of Fallot.
- Mild cases may cause no symptoms for years. Severe narrowing in a newborn causes cyanosis.

## Assessment
- A characteristic murmur is present.
- The infant or child may be completely without symptoms.
- Severe stenosis: cyanosis in the newborn, heart failure, and signs of decreased cardiac output (weak pulses, tiring, poor feeding, cool skin).

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airway, breathing and oxygenation first in a cyanotic or distressed infant.
2. Keep the infant calm and warm to cut oxygen demand.
3. Watch for heart failure and low cardiac output; give digoxin and diuretics as ordered.
4. Prepare the child and family for the procedure.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
- Non-surgical: the narrowed valve is stretched (dilated) during cardiac catheterization.
- Surgical: in infants, a closed transventricular valvotomy; in older children, a pulmonary valvotomy with cardiopulmonary bypass.

## Complications and red flags
- Heart failure, worsening cyanosis, fainting or poor perfusion.

## Client teaching
- Teach parents the signs of heart failure and low output, infection prevention, and that many children do well after valve dilation.

## How the exam asks about it
- Look for a murmur plus right ventricular hypertrophy. A cyanotic newborn with severe stenosis needs oxygen and urgent evaluation, not routine observation.

## Related topics
[[Congenital Heart Defects: Acyanotic Overview]], [[Cyanotic Heart Defects and Tetralogy of Fallot]], [[Heart Failure in Infants and Children]], [[Patent Ductus Arteriosus and Coarctation of the Aorta]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout gives no murmur description, no ductus management, and no recovery details. Confirm.

title: Cyanotic Heart Defects and Tetralogy of Fallot
body:
## Cyanotic defects
Blue blood (right to left) mixes into the body's supply. Examples: tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia, transposition of the great vessels.
- Signs: **central cyanosis**, clubbing, fatigue, poor growth, recurrent respiratory infection, squatting in older children, high hematocrit.
- Complications: clots and brain infarcts, heart failure.

## Tetralogy of Fallot (4 features)
- Pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, overriding aorta, VSD.
- Cyanosis at birth or in the first year, exertional dyspnea, slow weight gain.
- **Tet spell**: irritability, pallor, blackouts or convulsions.

## Priority actions in a tet spell
- Place the child in the **knee-chest** position (infants: side-lying with knees up; older children squat). Why: it raises systemic resistance and brings more blood to the lungs. Then oxygen, keep calm, warm, and give drugs as ordered.
- Promote rest, prevent infection, give digitalis/diuretics when ordered.

## Tricuspid atresia
- Tricuspid valve is closed; no flow from right atrium to right ventricle. Survival depends on a patent foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus.
- Cyanosis, tachycardia, dyspnea; older children have clubbing.
- **IV PGE1** keeps the ductus open. Surgery: vena cava-to-pulmonary shunt or Fontan-type procedure.

## Related topics
[[Congenital Heart Defects: Acyanotic Overview]], [[Pulmonary Stenosis]], [[Ventricular and Atrial Septal Defects]]
outlineRefs: Two Broad Classifications: Cyanotic Heart Defects

title: Choanal Atresia
body:
## What it is
- A congenital blockage at the back of the nasal passage (the choana), on one side (unilateral) or both (bilateral).
- Newborns breathe mostly through the nose, so a bilateral block is an airway emergency.

## Must-know facts
- **Danger sign**: cyanosis during feeding, because the nasal passage is blocked and the tongue can further restrict the airway. The color often improves when the baby cries, since the open mouth is used for breathing.
- Screening test (handout): close the baby's mouth and compress one nostril at a time; note distress. Failure to pass a small feeding catheter through the nares on either side establishes choanal atresia.

## Assessment
- Noisy breathing, cyanosis at rest or with feeding that clears with crying, retractions, nasal flaring.
- Inability to pass a catheter through the nose.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airway first: insert an **oral airway** to relieve breathing trouble temporarily (handout). Why: the infant can breathe through the mouth when it is kept open.
2. Keep the infant in a position that supports breathing and have suction available.
3. Monitor respirations and oxygen saturation.
4. Feed carefully; watch for color change.
5. Provide pre- and post-operative care and early screening.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
- Surgery perforates the atresia and then places a stent or repeated dilation to keep the new airway open.

## Complications and red flags
- Respiratory distress, apnea, aspiration during feeds.

## Client teaching
- Teach parents airway positioning, signs of breathing trouble, and care of the stent or airway as instructed.

## How the exam asks about it
- A newborn that turns blue when feeding but pink when crying: choanal atresia. Priority is an airway.

## Related topics
[[Congenital Anomaly Appraisal in the Newborn]], [[Newborn Assessment: Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, Neck and Chest]], [[Airway Management in the Primary Survey]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout does not give recovery details or follow-up. Confirm.

title: Tonsillitis, Adenoiditis and Tonsillectomy Care
body:
## What it is
Inflammation of lymphoid tissue in Waldeyer's ring. The usual cause is group A beta-hemolytic strep. Swollen tissue can obstruct breathing and swallowing; sore throat, altered smell, taste and hearing. Labs: leukocytosis, raised ESR.

## Why it matters
- Untreated strep can cause **acute glomerulonephritis** (5 to 21 days later) and **rheumatic fever** (2 to 6 weeks later), whose worst outcome is rheumatic heart disease, mainly the mitral valve.

## Surgery
- Antibiotics for the acute illness. Removal after 2 to 3 weeks if recurrent documented strep (handout: 4 per year) with swallowing and speech problems.
- Avoid surgery in children under about 5-6 years unless life-threatening, with bleeding disorders, or during acute respiratory infection.

## Post-op priorities (airway and bleeding first)
- Position **prone or side-lying** to drain secretions.
- Suction ready but do not suction unless obstructed.
- **Frequent swallowing = possible hemorrhage**. If bleeding, turn to the side and notify the doctor.
- Discourage coughing and throat clearing.
- Give clear, cool, non-citrus, non-carbonated fluids; avoid milk (coats the throat) and red liquids (look like blood).
- No straws, forks or sharp objects. Acetaminophen for pain.
- Teach: report bleeding, earache, fever; stay away from crowds until healed.

## Related topics
[[Epiglottitis]], [[Airway Management in the Primary Survey]]

title: Epiglottitis
body:
## What it is
Life-threatening inflammation of the epiglottis, classically by H. influenzae; a **medical emergency**.

## Assessment
- Sudden severe inspiratory stridor and hoarseness.
- Drooling and difficulty swallowing.
- Fever; high white count.
- **Tripod position**: leaning forward with chin thrust out and mouth open.

## Priority actions
1. Protect the airway: keep the child calm, do not leave unattended; prepare for intubation or tracheostomy.
2. **Never** examine the throat with a tongue blade or take a throat culture. Gagging can cause complete airway closure.
3. Give humidified oxygen and IV antibiotics (a third-generation cephalosporin).
4. Swelling usually decreases after about 24 hours; extubation around day 3 (handout).

## How the exam asks about it
A drooling, upright, anxious child: do NOT inspect the throat; call for help and prepare airway equipment.

## Related topics
[[Airway Management in the Primary Survey]], [[Respiratory Failure Recognition]], [[Tonsillitis, Adenoiditis and Tonsillectomy Care]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout says "children need moist air"; current practice focuses on securing the airway and avoiding upsetting the child.

title: Pediatric Bronchial Asthma and Status Asthmaticus
body:
## What it is
A chronic, **reversible** narrowing of the bronchi from allergens (extrinsic) or other triggers (intrinsic), causing bronchospasm and swelling.

## Signs
- Wheezing, **worse on expiration**; rapid labored breathing; dry hacking cough that becomes rattling with frothy clear sputum.

## Status asthmaticus
Distress that does not respond to vigorous treatment; can end in respiratory failure and death, so it is an emergency.

## Priority nursing actions
- **Upright position**; prepare for ventilation.
- Monitor vital signs, breath sounds, retractions, ABGs and oxygen saturation.
- Give oxygen, IV fluids and emergency drugs as ordered.
- Medications by nebulizer or metered-dose inhaler; use nebulizer if the child cannot use the MDI.
- Chest physiotherapy (clapping, vibration, postural drainage) is **not** for an acute attack.

## Drugs mentioned
- Albuterol (bronchodilator), cromolyn (preventive), inhaled corticosteroids. 

## Related topics
[[Respiratory Failure Recognition]], [[Breathing Assessment in the Primary Survey]], [[Epiglottitis]]

## Check against your textbook
The mild/moderate/severe drug scheme in the handout is simplified. Verify steps and dosing intervals using current guidelines.

title: Cleft Lip and Cleft Palate
body:
## What it is
Failure of tissues to fuse in embryo. Causes: heredity, radiation, rubella, chromosomal abnormalities, teratogens. Lip cleft ranges from a notch to complete separation to the nose; palate cleft affects the uvula, soft and hard palate.

## Pre-op feeding care
- Assess suck, swallow, secretions and breathing; monitor weight and intake.
- Enlarge the nipple, stimulate sucking, rest during feeding.
- Hold **upright**; direct formula to the **side and back** of the mouth.
- Position on the side after feeding; keep suction and a bulb syringe at the bedside. Encourage breastfeeding if possible.

## Surgery timing
- **Cheiloplasty** (lip) in the first weeks of life, before the palate.
- **Palatoplasty** (palate) between 12 and 18 months, before faulty speech develops.

## Post-op lip
- Lip protector taped to cheeks; lie on the back or side opposite the repair, **not prone**.
- Clean the suture line with normal saline after feeding.
- Prevent crying; keep the Logan bar dry.

## Post-op palate
- May lie prone. Feed by bottle, breast or cup.
- **No** tooth brushing, hard foods, oral suction, sharp objects or objects in the mouth. Soft elbow restraints may be used. Give analgesics.

## Related topics
[[Choanal Atresia]], [[Congenital Anomaly Appraisal in the Newborn]], [[Pyloric Stenosis]]

## Check against your textbook
Many sources place lip repair at about 2 to 3 months rather than the first weeks.

title: Pyloric Stenosis
body:
## What it is
- Overgrowth (hypertrophy) of the circular muscle of the pylorus narrows the channel between the stomach and the duodenum. Stenosis develops in the first few weeks of life.

## Must-know facts
- Because the block is **before** the bile duct entry, vomit is **non-bilious**.
- The infant is hungry and irritable after vomiting, since the stomach empties poorly.

## Assessment
- At about 4 to 6 weeks, the infant vomits soon after each feeding. Vomiting becomes increasingly forceful until **projectile**.
- Visible **peristaltic waves** moving left to right across the epigastrium during or just after a feed.
- **Olive-shaped mass** in the epigastrium just right of the navel.
- Signs of dehydration, malnutrition, and electrolyte imbalance (weight loss, sunken fontanel, fewer wet diapers, lethargy).

## Priority nursing actions
1. Monitor vital signs, intake and output, and weight. Why: dehydration is the main danger.
2. Check for signs of dehydration and electrolyte imbalance; give IV fluids as ordered.
3. **Withhold oral feedings** before surgery to prevent further electrolyte loss.
4. Give a pacifier to meet non-nutritive sucking needs while on IV fluids.
5. Prepare the child and family for surgery.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
- **Pyloromyotomy**: incision through the pyloric muscle fibers (may be laparoscopic).

## Complications and red flags
- Severe dehydration, metabolic alkalosis (added knowledge: loss of stomach acid), failure to thrive.

## Client teaching
- Teach parents about post-op feeding plans, wound care, and signs of vomiting after surgery.

## How the exam asks about it
- Projectile non-bilious vomiting in a young infant plus an olive-like mass: pyloric stenosis. Priority is hydration and electrolytes before surgery.
- Trap: bile-stained vomiting points to an obstruction below the bile duct, which is more urgent.

## Related topics
[[Duodenal Atresia and Imperforate Anus]], [[Hirschsprung's Disease]], [[Lactose Intolerance]]

## Check against your textbook
- Post-op feeding schedule and lab findings are not in the handout. Confirm.

title: Lactose Intolerance
body:
## What it is
- Inability to digest lactose (milk sugar) because the small intestine lacks enough **lactase**, the enzyme that splits lactose.
- Undigested lactose draws water into the bowel and ferments, causing the symptoms.

## Must-know facts
- Symptoms start after milk products are eaten.
- It is a food intolerance (enzyme problem), not a true allergy.

## Assessment
- Abdominal distention, crampy abdominal pain and colic, diarrhea, and excessive flatus after dairy.
- Ask about timing of symptoms after milk, cheese, ice cream; look at feeding history and growth.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Identify and remove the offending dairy product. Why: symptoms resolve when lactose is removed.
2. Make sure hydration is adequate if diarrhea is present.
3. Plan substitutions: soy-based formula in place of cow's milk formula or human milk (handout).
4. Replace lost nutrients: give calcium and vitamin D.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
- Enzyme tablets that predigest lactose or supplement the body's lactase may be used.

## Complications and red flags
- Poor growth or dehydration with heavy diarrhea; calcium and vitamin D deficiency if dairy is avoided without replacement.

## Client teaching
- Limit milk to one glass at a time and drink it with other foods rather than alone.
- Hard cheese, cottage cheese and yogurt are often better tolerated (the handout says they contain the inactive lactase enzyme).
- Small amounts of dairy each day can help colonic bacteria adapt.
- Teach parents to read labels for hidden lactose sources.

## How the exam asks about it
- Match symptom to cause: diarrhea and gas after milk equals lactase deficiency. The correct teaching is to modify the diet and supplement calcium and vitamin D, not to stop all dairy without replacements.

## Related topics
[[Celiac Disease]], [[Pyloric Stenosis]], [[Nutrition]]

## Check against your textbook
- Confirm how much dairy is tolerated and which products are safe; the handout gives no amounts.

title: Celiac Disease
body:
## What it is
Intolerance to **gluten**, a protein in barley, rye, oats and wheat (mnemonic B-R-O-W). It damages the intestinal lining, shrinks the villi, and blocks nutrient absorption. Symptoms appear about 3 to 6 months after gluten is started.

## Assessment
- Diarrhea (acute or slowly developing), **steatorrhea** (fatty stool), anorexia, abdominal pain and bloating, vomiting, muscle wasting especially in the buttocks and limbs.

## Celiac crisis
Triggered by infection, fasting or gluten: profuse watery diarrhea and vomiting, rapid dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, acidosis. This is the emergency to prioritize (fluids and electrolytes).

## Nursing care
- **Lifelong gluten-free diet**; use corn, rice and millet.
- Allowed: meat, fish, eggs, milk, vegetables, fruits, rice, corn products.
- Avoid: breads, cereals, pasta, crackers, cookies, beer, malted milk, prepared puddings, commercial ice cream.
- Supplement iron, folic acid and fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.

## Related topics
[[Lactose Intolerance]], [[Nutrition]], [[Hirschsprung's Disease]]

## Check against your textbook
Oats are debated as to gluten content. The handout's "toxic glutamine" explanation is an older idea.

title: Duodenal Atresia and Imperforate Anus
body:
## Duodenal atresia
- Part of the duodenum is missing or closed.
- **Early bilious vomiting**, no abdominal distention, vomiting continues even when not fed, few meconium stools then none.
- X-ray: **double bubble** sign (two air-filled spaces).
- Often linked to hydramnios and Down syndrome (added knowledge).

## Imperforate anus
- No meconium passed; anal canal absent or narrowed.
- Absent "wink" reflex around the anus; cannot insert a rubber catheter into the rectum.
- Abdominal distention develops.
- Repair depends on severity; a fistula to the bladder or vagina makes it harder.

## Nursing
- Check anal patency on the first newborn exam; report no stool in 24 hours; keep NPO and prepare for surgery.

## Related topics
[[Congenital Anomaly Appraisal in the Newborn]], [[Hirschsprung's Disease]], [[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]]

## Check against your textbook
Added: Down syndrome link with duodenal atresia. Surgery type is not described in the handout for duodenal atresia.

title: Hirschsprung's Disease
body:
## What it is
Absent nerve ganglion cells in part of the bowel (usually rectum), so that segment cannot move stool; the colon above enlarges (aganglionic megacolon).

## Assessment
- No meconium in the first 48 hours; symptoms within the first weeks.
- Abdominal bloating, bile-stained vomit, **ribbon-like** stools or small watery stools, fecal-smelling breath.
- Poor appetite, delayed growth, anemia.
- Diagnosis: abdominal X-ray, barium enema, rectal biopsy.

## Treatment
Surgical bowel resection / pull-through (around one year) and temporary colostomy.

## Post-op nursing
- Measure abdominal girth daily; check the incision and the stoma (red and moist is healthy).
- NPO until bowel sounds or flatus return (48-72 h); NG tube to intermittent suction; IV fluids, then advance diet.
- Teach colostomy and skin care.

## Related topics
[[Down Syndrome]], [[Duodenal Atresia and Imperforate Anus]], [[Celiac Disease]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout says low-fiber, high-calorie, high-protein diet; verify. Pre-op irrigations with saline are mentioned.

title: Abdominal Wall Defects: Omphalocele, Gastroschisis and Umbilical Hernia
body:
## Omphalocele
Bowel or organs protrude through the umbilical ring **inside a translucent sac**. Cover the sac right after birth with sterile gauze soaked in warm saline to prevent drying.

## Gastroschisis
Bowel protrudes **lateral to the umbilical ring with no covering membrane**. Cover loosely with saline-soaked pads and wrap in plastic drape; surgery within hours. The handout says position supine and keep the bowel moist.

## Umbilical hernia
Small muscle defect lets peritoneum bulge at the navel, more obvious with crying. Usually closes by age 3 without treatment. Repair indications: strangulation, no closure by age 4-5, very large defect under 2, or cosmetic. Coins or binders do not help.

## Priority
Protect exposed tissue from infection, drying and heat loss before surgery.

## Related topics
[[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]], [[Inguinal Hernia and Hydrocele]], [[Congenital Anomaly Appraisal in the Newborn]]

## Check against your textbook
Gastroschisis positioning is often side-lying to protect bowel blood supply; verify.

title: Talipes (Clubfoot)
body:
## What it is
- **Talipes**, popularly clubfoot, is a congenital foot deformity. It is more frequent in boys, probably inherited in a polygenic pattern, and is usually one foot (unilateral).
- Four true types:
  - **Plantar flexion** (equinus or "horsefoot"): forefoot lower than the heel.
  - **Dorsiflexion**: heel lower than the forefoot, or the front of the foot flexed toward the leg.
  - **Varus**: the foot turns in.
  - **Valgus**: the foot turns out.

## Must-know facts
- Correction works best when started in the newborn period.
- Casts are applied with the foot placed in an **overcorrected** position and are changed every 1 to 2 weeks because infants grow quickly.
- The final cast is removed after about **6 weeks** (timing varies).

## Assessment
- Observe foot position and flexibility at birth; compare both feet; note whether the foot can be passively moved to neutral.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Start treatment early (manipulation, stretching, serial casting).
2. After each cast: check circulation, color, warmth, movement, sensation and skin edges (neurovascular checks). Why: swelling under a cast can cut off blood flow.
3. Teach cast care: keep dry, watch for odor, drainage or tightness, do not insert objects.
4. After casting, teach parents passive range-of-motion exercises, putting the foot and ankle through full range several times a day for months.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
- **Denis Browne-type splints** maintain correction. Surgery (most often a **posteromedial release**) is used when casting does not succeed.

## Complications and red flags
- Pain, swelling, toes that are cold, blue or pale, or numb; skin breakdown; relapse of the deformity.

## Client teaching
- Keep follow-up visits; do the exercises daily; return promptly for any cast problem.

## How the exam asks about it
- Identify type from the description (equinus vs varus). Priority after casting is a neurovascular check.

## Related topics
[[Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip]], [[Cast Care and Neurovascular Checks]], [[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout does not name the Ponseti method; confirm current practice and cast schedule.

title: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
body:
## What it is
A shallow or flat acetabulum, so the femoral head does not sit in the socket. Causes: genetics and maternal hormones, mechanical factors like **breech** position, newborn ligament laxity.

## Assessment
- **Barlow test**: pushes the hip backward; slipping out is positive (unstable).
- **Ortolani maneuver**: reduces a dislocated hip; a palpable "clunk" as it goes back in. 
- Uneven leg creases, a **Galeazzi sign** (one knee lower), limited abduction.

## Management
- Hip held **flexed and abducted** to deepen the socket: multiple diapers, splints, casts. A few need surgery with a pin.
- Early detection is best.

## Nursing
Teach parents how to apply and care for the device; skin checks; do not narrow the diapering position.

## Related topics
[[Talipes (Clubfoot)]], [[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's Barlow/Ortolani wording is jumbled. Pavlik harness, the standard device, is not named.

title: Hypospadias and Epispadias
body:
## What it is
- A congenital condition with the urethral opening in the wrong place.
- **Hypospadias**: the opening is on the underside (ventral surface) of the penis, behind the glans.
- **Epispadias**: the opening is on the top (dorsal surface).
- **Chordee**: ventral curvature of the penis, often with hypospadias; it causes constriction.

## Must-know facts
- If the opening is only slightly displaced and still on the glans, no treatment is needed.
- Hypospadias is the more common of the two (added knowledge).

## Assessment
- Visible malposition of the urethral orifice.
- Inability to make a straight stream of urine.
- Careful, thorough genitourinary exam of every newborn.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Identify and document the abnormal meatus at the first newborn exam.
2. Report it before any circumcision. Why: foreskin tissue may be needed for surgical repair (added knowledge; ask what the provider wants).
3. Assess voiding and urine stream.
4. Prepare the child and family for surgery, and give post-op care (urinary drainage, wound care).

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
- Surgical repair (urethroplasty) for severe cases, done at about two to three years in the handout (around toilet training) or before kindergarten.

## Complications and red flags
- Urinary tract infection, painful or difficult voiding, sexual or fertility problems if untreated.

## Client teaching
- Explain the plan and timing of surgery; teach post-op care, avoiding trauma, and hygiene.

## How the exam asks about it
- Dorsal opening = epispadias; ventral = hypospadias.
- Trap: advice to circumcise before evaluation.

## Memory aid
Hypo = under (below); Epi = on top.

## Related topics
[[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]], [[Cryptorchidism and the Cremasteric Reflex]], [[Inguinal Hernia and Hydrocele]]

## Check against your textbook
- Current practice repairs earlier (about 6 to 18 months). Circumcision advice is added; confirm.

title: Inguinal Hernia and Hydrocele
body:
## What it is
- **Inguinal hernia**: the processus vaginalis (the tube between the abdomen and scrotum in the fetus) fails to close completely, so part of the intestine can descend into the groin or scrotum.
- **Hydrocele**: fluid in the scrotal sac.

## Must-know facts
- **Non-communicating hydrocele**: seen at birth; leftover peritoneal fluid is trapped in the lower part of the processus vaginalis; **needs no treatment**.
- **Communicating hydrocele**: the processus vaginalis stays open from the scrotum to the abdominal cavity; it is associated with a hernia.
- Umbilical hernia is different (a muscle defect at the navel); see [[Abdominal Wall Defects: Omphalocele, Gastroschisis and Umbilical Hernia]].

## Assessment
- A bulge in the groin or scrotum, often more visible when the baby cries or strains.
- A hydrocele is a smooth, painless scrotal swelling.
- Signs of strangulation (added knowledge): firm, tender, discolored bulge, vomiting, irritability, no stool.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Assess the groin and scrotum with each newborn exam and document.
2. Report a hernia that cannot be reduced or is painful immediately. Why: trapped bowel loses its blood supply.
3. Prepare the child and family for surgery when ordered; give routine post-op care.
4. Teach parents about when to seek urgent help.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
- Hernias are repaired surgically. Non-communicating hydroceles are watched and usually disappear.

## Complications and red flags
- Incarceration or strangulation of bowel; vomiting with a firm tender bulge.

## Client teaching
- Teach parents to check for the bulge when the child cries, and to go to the emergency department if the bulge is hard, painful, or the child vomits.

## How the exam asks about it
- Decide which finding needs no treatment (non-communicating hydrocele) and which needs surgery (communicating, hernia).

## Related topics
[[Hypospadias and Epispadias]], [[Cryptorchidism and the Cremasteric Reflex]], [[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout does not give repair timing or strangulation signs. These are added; confirm.

title: Truncus Arteriosus and Transposition of the Great Vessels
body:
## What it is
- Both are **cyanotic** congenital heart defects. The handout only names them in its list (tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia, transposition of the great vessels), so the details below are general textbook knowledge, kept simple.
- **Truncus arteriosus**: one large vessel leaves the heart instead of separate aorta and pulmonary artery, so blood mixes.
- **Transposition of the great vessels**: the aorta and pulmonary artery are switched, so body blood circulates again without reaching the lungs.

## Must-know facts
- Common to all cyanotic defects in the handout: central cyanosis, clubbing, easy tiring, slow growth, repeated respiratory infections, squatting in older children, raised hematocrit.
- Blood from the right side of the heart reaches the body without being oxygenated (right-to-left mixing), so oxygen level stays low.
- The body makes more red cells to compensate, which is why hematocrit rises and clots become a danger.

## Assessment
- Blue color (central, lips and tongue) that does not clear with crying or oxygen, fatigue with feeding, fast breathing.
- Older children: clubbed fingers, exertional dyspnea, squatting to rest.
- Look for signs of heart failure: moist cough, sweating, enlarged liver.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airway, breathing and oxygenation first (ABC): position for easy breathing, give oxygen as ordered.
2. Keep the child calm and warm; crying and cold raise oxygen demand.
3. Cluster care so the child can rest.
4. Give digoxin and diuretics only as ordered (check apical rate before digoxin).
5. Prevent infection and keep the child well hydrated (thick blood clots more easily).

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
- Surgery is the definitive treatment and varies by defect. Newborns with a ductus-dependent circulation may receive an IV prostaglandin (PGE1) to keep the ductus open until surgery, as the handout states for tricuspid atresia.

## Complications and red flags
- Brain infarction and blood clots; heart failure; worsening blue color or limpness.

## Client teaching
- Teach parents to recognize color change and feeding fatigue, keep up with infection prevention, and report fever or vomiting early because dehydration thickens blood.

## How the exam asks about it
- A blue infant or clubbed child: this is a cyanotic defect. Priority is oxygenation and calm, not a feeding schedule.
- Trap: choosing a long-term teaching answer when a breathing problem is the immediate issue.

## Related topics
[[Cyanotic Heart Defects and Tetralogy of Fallot]], [[Tricuspid Atresia]], [[Heart Failure in Infants and Children]], [[Congenital Heart Defects: Acyanotic Overview]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout gives no definition, murmur, treatment, or timing for truncus arteriosus or transposition. Confirm the anatomy, the surgery names and the role of prostaglandin for each.

title: Tricuspid Atresia
body:
## What it is
- The tricuspid valve is completely closed, so no blood flows from the right atrium into the right ventricle. It is a very serious cyanotic defect.
- The child survives only while the **foramen ovale** and the **ductus arteriosus** stay open, because they let blood cross to the left side and reach the lungs.

## Must-know facts
- Signs: cyanosis, tachycardia, dyspnea. Older children show chronic low oxygen and finger clubbing.
- Part of the cyanotic group with tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus and transposition.

## Assessment
- Blue skin and lips, fast heart rate, labored breathing.
- Poor feeding and fatigue; later, growth delay and clubbing.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Support oxygenation and airway first (ABC).
2. Keep the ductus open: an **IV infusion of PGE1** is started as ordered. Why: closure of the ductus would cut off the only route of blood to the lungs.
3. Keep the infant calm, warm, and resting.
4. Monitor oxygen saturation, heart rate, breathing and perfusion closely.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
- Surgery is staged. The handout names a **vena cava-to-pulmonary artery shunt**, which sends more blood to the lungs, and a **Fontan procedure** (also described as a Glenn shunt baffle), which reorganizes the right side of the heart.

## Complications and red flags
- Worsening cyanosis, limpness, poor perfusion: these suggest the ductus is closing and need urgent reporting.

## Client teaching
- Teach parents to watch color, feeding and breathing, to protect against infection, and to keep appointments before and after surgery.

## How the exam asks about it
- Newborn with cyanosis and a closed tricuspid valve: the key action is PGE1 to keep the ductus patent.
- Trap: a drug that closes the ductus (such as indomethacin for PDA) would be harmful here.

## Related topics
[[Cyanotic Heart Defects and Tetralogy of Fallot]], [[Truncus Arteriosus and Transposition of the Great Vessels]], [[Patent Ductus Arteriosus and Coarctation of the Aorta]], [[Heart Failure in Infants and Children]]

## Check against your textbook
- Confirm the staged surgeries, the exact meaning of "Glenn shunt baffle", and PGE1 dosing; the handout gives no numbers.

title: Piaget's Stages of Cognitive Development
body:
## What it is
Piaget described how children think at each age. Each stage changes how the nurse should explain things.

## Must-know facts
- **Sensorimotor (birth to about 2 years)**, split in the handout into circular reactions:
  - 1 to 4 months: primary circular reaction (the infant's own body is the center of attention).
  - 4 to 8 months: secondary circular reaction (attention moves from the body to the environment).
  - 8 to 12 months: coordination of secondary reactions.
  - 12 to 18 months: tertiary circular reaction (trial and error).
- **Preoperational (about 2 to 7 years)**: thought becomes symbolic; answers can be reached mentally instead of by trying things physically; understands simple abstractions but thinking is concrete and literal; **egocentric** (cannot take another's view). Preschool features: **centering** (sees one feature only, such as the banana being yellow but not long), **magical thinking** (animals and objects think and feel).
- **Concrete operational (about 7 to 12 years)**: systematic reasoning, classifying objects by color or other attributes, and **reversibility** (can follow a maze and retrace the steps). Reasoning is **inductive**, from specific to general (this toy is plastic and broke, so all plastic toys break easily).
- **Formal operational (about 12 and up)**: solves hypothetical problems with scientific reasoning, understands cause and effect, deals with past, present and future, adult-like thought.

## Priority nursing actions
- Match the explanation to the stage: show and let infants handle safe objects; give toddlers and preschoolers short, literal, simple wording; give school-age children step-by-step reasons; give adolescents full explanations and talk time.
- Why: a child can only learn what the nervous system is mature enough to understand.

## Complications and red flags
- Failure to reach age-expected thinking can mean delayed development; compare with milestones.

## Client teaching
- Teach parents that a young child's "no" or magical beliefs are normal thinking, not misbehavior.

## How the exam asks about it
- A preschooler thinks an injection is punishment: that is magical thinking and egocentrism. Answer: simple reassurance that it is not a punishment.
- A school-age child who follows steps backward shows reversibility.

## Memory aid
Sensorimotor, Preoperational, Concrete, Formal: "Some Pupils Can Fly" (made-up aid).

## Related topics
[[Childhood Age Periods and Developmental Theories]], [[Preschooler Development and Thinking]], [[School-Age Child Development]], [[Kohlberg's Stages of Moral Development]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout labels formal operations as "12 yr"; textbooks often give 11 or 12 and up. Confirm age boundaries.

title: Kohlberg's Stages of Moral Development
body:
## What it is
Kohlberg described how reasons for right and wrong change with age.

## Must-know facts
- **Infancy (handout)**: a pre-moral or pre-religious time; infants learn that some actions bring affection and approval, others bring scolding.
- **Level I, pre-conventional**:
  - Stage 1 (about 2 to 3 years): behavior is motivated by punishment and reward.
  - Stage 2 (about 4 to 7 years): individualism; acts to satisfy own needs rather than society's.
- **Level II, conventional (about 7 to 10 years)**: interpersonal relationships and mutuality; the child follows rules to be a good person in his or her own eyes and in others' eyes.
- **Level III, post-conventional (older than about 12)**: social contract and utilitarian law-making (following society's standards for the good of all), and universal ethical principles (following internalized standards of conduct).
- Many adults never reach the top level.

## Priority nursing actions
- Toddlers and preschoolers: use praise, clear limits and consequences; explain simply.
- School-age: appeal to being "good" and following rules; give them rules to follow in care.
- Adolescents: they see self-care as adult behavior, so involve them in decisions and allow them responsibility.

## How the exam asks about it
- A child cooperates only for a sticker or to avoid punishment: pre-conventional.
- A child follows hospital rules to be seen as good: conventional.
- Trap: mixing Kohlberg levels with Piaget stages. Kohlberg is about morals, Piaget about thinking.

## Memory aid
Three levels: Pre (punishment/needs), Conventional (good person), Post (principles).

## Related topics
[[Piaget's Stages of Cognitive Development]], [[Childhood Age Periods and Developmental Theories]], [[Adolescent Development]], [[School-Age Child Development]]

## Check against your textbook
- Age boundaries differ among books. The handout's ages for the stages overlap (2-3, 4-7, 7-10, over 12); confirm them.

title: Fears, Play and Toys by Age Group
body:
## What it is
A quick table of the typical fear, play type and toys for each age. These are classic exam recall items.

## Must-know facts
- **Infant**: fear of strangers (stranger anxiety); **solitary** play; sensory toys such as a mobile, rattle, musical toys and crib toys.
- **Toddler**: fear of **separation**; **parallel** play (side by side, not together); push and pull toys.
- **Preschooler**: fear of **mutilation and castration** (body injury); **associative** play plus imitation or make-believe; simple puzzles, dolls, coloring books.
- **School-age**: fear of displacement from school (being kept away); **indoor competitive** play; computer games and table games.
- **Adolescent**: fear of displacement from peers; **outdoor competitive** play (athletics and sports); basketball and similar.

## Priority nursing actions
- Infant: keep parents or one consistent caregiver near, give pacifier and sensory toys.
- Toddler: keep a parent present, allow a favorite object, offer choices, keep routines.
- Preschooler: explain simply, let the child touch equipment, use dolls to show procedures, reassure that illness is not punishment.
- School-age: arrange for schoolwork, games and contact with classmates.
- Adolescent: support peer contact, privacy and involvement in choices.
- Why: each age-specific fear drives distress during hospitalization; meeting the need lowers fear and improves cooperation.

## How the exam asks about it
