- Pick the activity for a hospitalized child of a given age. Match the play type: parallel for toddlers, competitive for school-age.
- Trap: choosing a team sport for a toddler or a push toy for an adolescent.

## Memory aid
Play types in order: Solitary, Parallel, Associative, then Competitive (made-up aid: "S-P-A-C").

## Related topics
[[Infant Development, Fears and Play]], [[Toddler Development and Toilet Training]], [[Preschooler Development and Thinking]], [[School-Age Child Development]], [[Adolescent Development]]

## Check against your textbook
- Some books add cooperative play for school-age; the handout lists competitive. Preschool age is given as 3 to 5 in the stage notes.

title: Cryptorchidism and the Cremasteric Reflex
body:
## What it is
- **Cryptorchidism**: one or both testes are not in the scrotum. Causes named in the handout: **agenesis** (the testis never formed), **ectopic** testis, or **undescended** testis.
- The **cremasteric reflex** is elicited by stroking the inner thigh; the testis on that side rises. The handout says it tests spinal nerves T8-T10 and may be absent in newborns younger than 10 days.

## Must-know facts
- In a newborn exam both testes should be present in the scrotum. Premature boys often have undescended testes, which can be normal for gestational age.
- The handout links absent testes to the kidneys: testes arise from the same embryonic tissue, so a boy with agenesis is referred for kidney anomalies.

## Assessment
- Inspect and gently palpate the scrotum; note an empty or small scrotal sac; compare sides.
- Check the urethral opening location as part of the same exam (see [[Hypospadias and Epispadias]]).

## Priority nursing actions
1. Report an absent testis, because it needs further evaluation (and, per the handout, a kidney check).
2. Document findings clearly (side, location).
3. Teach parents that follow-up is needed even if the testis may descend by itself in a premature infant.

## Complications and red flags
- Sudden pain, redness or swelling of a testis at any age is an emergency to report immediately (testicular torsion; added knowledge).

## How the exam asks about it
- Empty scrotum in a newborn: report and expect evaluation; do not assume it is normal unless the infant is premature.
- Reasoning: absent testis -> think kidney anomaly.

## Related topics
[[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]], [[Hypospadias and Epispadias]], [[Inguinal Hernia and Hydrocele]]

## Check against your textbook
- Many texts give the cremasteric reflex nerve as L1-L2, not T8-T10. Verify. Treatment (orchiopexy) and timing are not in the handout.

title: Congenital Torticollis, Achondroplasia and Digit Anomalies
body:
## What it is
Short newborn-exam clues from the handout that point to a structural or genetic problem.

## Must-know facts
- **Neck**: short and chubby with skin folds is normal. **Rigidity** of the neck may signal **congenital torticollis** (a shortened neck muscle) or **meningitis** (see [[Bacterial Meningitis and Encephalitis]]).
- **Extremities**:
  - Unusually **short arms** suggest **achondroplasia**, a form of short-limbed dwarfism.
  - A **simian crease** (single horizontal palm line) may signal Down syndrome.
  - **Syndactyly** is webbing of fingers or toes.
  - **Polydactyly** is extra fingers or toes.

## Assessment
- Look at head position and neck movement; compare arm and leg length; open the hand and look at the palm; count digits.

## Priority nursing actions
1. A stiff neck with fever or irritability is treated as possible meningitis first: report immediately and prepare for isolation per orders. Why: it is life-threatening and infectious.
2. Otherwise document the structural finding and report to the provider.
3. Support the family: explain what was found, and avoid guessing a diagnosis.

## Complications and red flags
- Torticollis may delay normal head control; severe or untreated cases need therapy (added knowledge).

## How the exam asks about it
- Match each finding to its condition: simian crease -> Down syndrome; short limbs -> achondroplasia; neck rigidity -> torticollis or meningitis.

## Related topics
[[Down Syndrome]], [[Newborn Assessment: Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, Neck and Chest]], [[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout does not give treatment or cause for torticollis or achondroplasia. Confirm management (stretching, positioning, orthopedic care) in your text.

title: Eisenmenger Syndrome
body:
## What it is
- A late complication of a left-to-right shunt such as a **VSD**. Long-standing extra blood flow into the lungs raises pressure in the lung vessels (pulmonary hypertension) until the shunt **reverses to right-to-left**.
- Once blood flows right to left, unoxygenated blood enters the body and the child turns blue.

## Must-know facts
- The handout lists it under VSD: pulmonary hypertension and respiratory failure may occur, and a reverse (right-to-left) shunt may develop.
- A VSD is the most common congenital heart defect (about 30% in the handout).

## Assessment
- Newly developed blue color (cyanosis), exertional dyspnea, fatigue, clubbing.
- Earlier signs of the shunt: loud systolic murmur, repeated respiratory infections, poor weight gain.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Support oxygenation and breathing (ABC); report new cyanosis at once.
2. Limit exertion and cluster care to save energy.
3. Prevent infection; monitor for heart failure.
4. Teach the family that repairing defects early prevents this complication.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
- Early closure of the defect (device in catheterization or open repair on bypass) before pressure damage occurs. Once reversal has happened, repair is generally no longer helpful (added knowledge).

## Complications and red flags
- Respiratory failure, heart failure, worsening cyanosis.

## How the exam asks about it
- A child with a known VSD who becomes cyanotic: think shunt reversal. Priority: oxygen and notify the provider.

## Related topics
[[Ventricular and Atrial Septal Defects]], [[Congenital Heart Defects: Acyanotic Overview]], [[Heart Failure in Infants and Children]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout does not describe treatment or prognosis of Eisenmenger syndrome. Confirm it.

title: Rheumatic Fever and Glomerulonephritis After Strep Throat
body:
## What it is
- Two delayed complications of untreated or partly treated **group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal** infection of the throat. The handout lists them under tonsillitis.
- **Acute glomerulonephritis**: kidney inflammation that appears about **5 to 21 days** after the strep infection.
- **Rheumatic fever**: appears about **2 to 6 weeks** after the infection. Its most serious outcome is **rheumatic heart disease**, damage to the heart valves, especially the **mitral valve**.

## Must-know facts
- Tonsillitis labs: leukocytosis and raised ESR.
- Both happen because the body reacts to the strep infection, so the best prevention is **full treatment of strep throat** with the entire antibiotic course.
- Other increased risks: recurrent strep with documented infection (handout: 4 times a year) leads to tonsillectomy consideration.

## Assessment
- Sore throat, enlarged tonsils, difficulty swallowing; a history of recent strep.
- Watch for later signs: cola-colored or reduced urine, puffy face, high blood pressure (kidney); joint pain, fever, new murmur or chest symptoms (heart; added knowledge).

## Priority nursing actions
1. Make sure the child takes the **entire** prescribed antibiotic course even when symptoms improve. Why: stopping early leaves bacteria that trigger complications.
2. Monitor for airway obstruction and swallowing difficulty.
3. Teach parents which late symptoms to report.

## Complications and red flags
- Rheumatic heart disease (valve damage, heart failure); kidney injury.

## Client teaching
- Finish all antibiotics; return if urine changes, swelling, joint pain or breathlessness appear; follow-up care.

## How the exam asks about it
- Which teaching prevents rheumatic fever? Completing the antibiotics.
- Timing facts: AGN about 5-21 days, rheumatic fever about 2-6 weeks.

## Related topics
[[Tonsillitis, Adenoiditis and Tonsillectomy Care]], [[Acute Glomerulonephritis (Nephritic Syndrome)]], [[Heart Failure in Infants and Children]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout gives only the timing and the final complication. Confirm full criteria, treatment and long-term prevention for rheumatic fever.

title: Scalp Swellings in the Newborn: Caput, Cephalhematoma and Craniotabes
body:
## What it is
Three different newborn head findings from birth pressure. They look similar but differ in cause, location and how long they last.

## Must-know facts
- **Caput succedaneum**: swelling of the scalp from a prolonged labor; it **crosses over the suture lines**; goes away by about the third day of life.
- **Cephalhematoma**: a blood collection under the periosteum from rupture of small vessels with the pressure of birth; absorbed in **3 to 6 weeks**. (It does not cross suture lines; this is general textbook teaching, not in the handout.)
- **Craniotabes**: localized swelling or softening of cranial bones from pressure of the fetal skull against the mother's pelvic bone; **corrects itself** without treatment.

## Assessment
- Palpate the scalp: soft puffy swelling over suture lines points to caput; a firm, defined swelling confined to one bone points to cephalhematoma.
- Also assess the fontanels: anterior soft, flat and diamond-shaped (closes 12 to 18 months), posterior triangular (closes in 2 to 3 months).

## Priority nursing actions
1. Observe and document size and location; no special treatment is needed for any of the three.
2. Watch the cephalhematoma for jaundice later (blood breakdown; added knowledge).
3. Reassure parents the swelling is expected to resolve; avoid pressing or rubbing.

## Complications and red flags
- A bulging fontanel or widely separated sutures suggest raised pressure (see [[Hydrocephalus]]) and are not normal.

## How the exam asks about it
- "Crosses suture lines" = caput. "Blood, 3-6 weeks" = cephalhematoma.

## Memory aid
Caput = Crosses; Cephalhematoma = Confined (made-up aid).

## Related topics
[[Newborn Assessment: Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, Neck and Chest]], [[Gestational Age Estimation and Newborn Measurements]], [[Hydrocephalus]]

## Check against your textbook
- The suture-line rule for cephalhematoma and jaundice risk are textbook additions. Confirm.

title: Umbilical Cord Assessment
body:
## What it is
Checking the newborn's cord stump for normal structure, healing and signs of anomaly.

## Must-know facts
- Normal stump: white, gelatinous, with **2 arteries and 1 vein** (the blue and red streaks seen in the handout).
- A **single umbilical artery** may signal a congenital heart or kidney anomaly, or a chromosomal trisomy (if other findings agree).
- The cord should separate (break free) by about **day 6 to 10**.
- If an **umbilical hernia** is present, taping the cord or placing buttons or coins on it does **not** help the defect close.
- Bowel sounds should be present 1 hour after birth; a scaphoid (sunken) abdomen could indicate missing contents.

## Assessment
- Count the vessels at birth; inspect the stump for dryness, redness, drainage, odor, bleeding; look at the skin around it.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Count the vessels; report one artery.
2. Keep the cord clean, dry and exposed to air, folded below the diaper (general teaching; verify local policy).
3. Report redness, pus, foul smell or bleeding. Why: the cord is a direct route for infection.
4. Teach parents not to apply home remedies or coins over a hernia.

## Complications and red flags
- Infection (omphalitis), bleeding, prolonged non-separation.

## How the exam asks about it
- Two arteries and one vein = normal. Number counts and "coin on hernia" distractors are common.

## Related topics
[[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]], [[Abdominal Wall Defects: Omphalocele, Gastroschisis and Umbilical Hernia]], [[Congenital Anomaly Appraisal in the Newborn]]

## Check against your textbook
- Cord care methods (dry care versus antiseptic) differ by facility. Confirm local practice.

title: Maternal Bonding and Language Development
body:
## What it is
- **Maternal bonding**: a special mutual relationship between mother and infant.
- **Language development**: expected vocabulary at each age.

## Must-know facts
- Bonding is best started **immediately after birth** and can be achieved **within the first 30 minutes**.
- Handout vocabulary: about **900 words at 3 years, 1500 at 4 years, 2100 at 5 years**.
- Toddlers ask questions constantly (up to 400 a day in the handout) and use "no" often.

## Assessment
- Watch eye contact, touching, talking to the infant, and feeding behavior at the first contact.
- Compare a child's speech with the vocabulary expected for age.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Support early skin-to-skin contact and first feeding if mother and baby are stable. Why: it begins attachment and keeps the newborn warm.
2. Do not separate a stable mother and newborn for routine tasks.
3. Talk, read and sing with infants and children.
4. Refer a child with lagging speech for hearing and developmental evaluation.

## Client teaching
- Encourage parents to hold, talk, and respond to cries; explain that bonding can still develop later if early contact was missed (added knowledge).

## How the exam asks about it
- When should bonding begin? Right after birth, within the first 30 minutes.
- Match the vocabulary count to the age.

title: Heart Failure in Infants and Children
body:
## What it is
Congestive heart failure (CHF) is the most common complication of congenital heart defects. The heart cannot pump enough blood for the body's needs.

## Must-know facts
- Signs listed in the handout: tachycardia, tachypnea, profuse **scalp sweating**, fatigue, irritability, respiratory distress, feeding problems, poor weight gain or failure to thrive, frequent respiratory infections and cough, hepatomegaly from blood backing up.
- In respiratory distress: moist cough, diaphoresis, severe dyspnea. Sweating on the brow during feeding or crying shows easy fatigue.
- Acyanotic defects (VSD, ASD, PDA) with large shunts overload the lungs; coarctation causes strain from high pressure.

## Assessment
- Heart rate, respiratory rate, work of breathing, color, sweating with feeds, weight trend, liver size, urine output.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airway, breathing, oxygen as ordered; upright or semi-upright position to ease breathing.
2. Reduce energy use: cluster care, small frequent feedings, minimize crying.
3. Give digoxin and diuretics as ordered; check apical pulse for a full minute before digoxin and hold per parameters.
4. Weigh daily and record intake and output.
5. Prevent infection.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
- Digoxin and diuretics (handout for coarctation); correction of the defect by catheterization or surgery.

## Complications and red flags
- Worsening distress, falling urine output, poor feeding, new cyanosis.

## How the exam asks about it
- A baby who tires and sweats during feeding: suspect heart failure. Priority is to support breathing and conserve energy.
